slides.0.title: Theory exams: writing short answers and essays
slides.0.subtitle: Understand what the question asks before deciding what to write
slides.1.title: Command words
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Describe
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Say what something is: features, rules, practices. No need to explain why, but be specific (numbers, names, years)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Explain
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Say why: link every fact to a cause and effect, e.g. “cool → acidity retained → suits sparkling”. Listing facts alone loses marks
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Compare
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Cover similarities and differences on both sides at once; put both side by side on every axis (climate, variety, winemaking, market)
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Assess / discuss
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Needs arguments, evidence, counter-arguments and a conclusion; the conclusion must be a conditional verdict, not a summary
slides.1.content: See “explain”, write causes; see “assess”, give a verdict: the command word decides how marks are given.
slides.2.title: Answer structure and timing
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Skeleton first
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Spend a minute or two listing points and examples before writing; a skeleton keeps you on track and shows the examiner your structure at a glance
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Paragraph formula
slides.2.highlights.1.content: One point per paragraph: claim → fact (with year or figure) → mechanism → effect on style or market
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Allocate time by marks
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Allocate time by marks; better to reach the main points in every question than to spend everything on the first; leave time to check consistent spelling and dated figures
slides.2.content: Examiners look at how many marking points you cover, not word count.
slides.3.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
When a question starts with “explain”, what matters most?
A. Writing only a conclusion
B. Avoiding all numbers
C. Linking every fact to cause and effect
D. Listing as many facts as possible
Listing facts alone loses marks.
What is the best conclusion for an “assess” question?
A. Restating every point
B. Introducing new facts
C. No conclusion
D. A conditional verdict
Judge by dimension, then give an overall view.
Short answer: explain why top sparkling-wine regions tend to be in cool climates. (about 150 words)
Cool conditions keep acidity high
Lower sugar → low-alcohol base wine
The second fermentation adds more alcohol, so the base must be low in alcohol
More neutral aromas carry winemaking flavours such as autolysis
Example: Champagne, England or Tasmania

A cool climate ripens grapes slowly, keeping acidity high and sugar low, giving high-acid, low-alcohol, neutral base wine. The second fermentation adds roughly another 1–1.5% alcohol, so the base must be low in alcohol; high acidity carries the freshness of the bubbles, and neutral aromas let autolysis and age take the lead. Champagne, England and Tasmania are examples.
Short answer: compare the pros and cons of bush vines and VSP trellising. (about 150 words)
Bush vines: no wires, low cost, drought-tolerant
Bush vines: the canopy shades fruit, suiting hot regions
Bush vines: hard to mechanise, poorer airflow
VSP: even light and airflow, less disease
VSP: suits machinery but needs investment in trellis

Bush vines need no wires, are cheap and drought-tolerant, and their canopy shades the fruit, suiting hot, dry Mediterranean regions, but they are hard to mechanise and have poorer airflow. VSP gives even light and airflow, less disease and easy mechanisation, but needs trellis investment and fruit can sunburn in hot regions. The choice depends on climate, labour cost and style goals.
